back: The degree to which the result meets requirements and stakeholder expectations.
Quality: how well requirements are met. Grade: a category of features. Low grade can be acceptable; low quality is always a problem.
Quality is planned and built in. Preventing defects costs less than finding and fixing them.
Assurance: the process (audits), aims to prevent defects. Control: the deliverables (inspection, testing), aims to find defects.
A structured, independent review of whether project activities comply with policies, processes and procedures. Usually done by a team outside the project.
Examining a work product to determine whether it conforms to documented standards. Also used to verify defect repairs.
Describes how the organization's quality policies and procedures will be applied to achieve the project's quality objectives.
The specific attributes to measure and how compliance will be verified, such as failure rate or defects per day.
A project document with quality issues, recommendations for corrective action and a summary of quality control findings.
Also called a fishbone or Ishikawa diagram. Branches possible causes off a problem statement to find the root cause.
Shows measurements over time against a mean and upper and lower control limits, to tell whether a process is stable.
Control limits: calculated from the process data. Specification limits: the maximum and minimum allowed by the requirements.
Seven points in a row on one side of the mean indicate the process is out of control, even if all are within the control limits.
Bars sorted from most to least frequent cause. Shows the vital few: about 80% of problems come from 20% of causes.
Plots one variable against another to show whether they are related.
A bar chart showing how often each value occurs: the distribution of the data.
A map of the steps and decision points of a process. Also called a process map.
An ongoing effort to improve processes and products in small steps. Approaches: plan-do-check-act (PDCA), Lean, Total Quality Management, Six Sigma.
Buyer: purchases products or services. Seller (vendor, contractor, supplier): provides them.
Determines whether work is best done by the project team or purchased from outside sources.
Plan the procurements; conduct them (select a seller and award the contract); monitor and control them (manage performance and close the contract).
The description of what the seller must deliver.
RFI: gather information from the market. RFP: ask sellers to propose a solution to a complex need. RFQ: ask for a price when price is the main factor.
A meeting where the buyer answers sellers' questions, so that all bidders receive the same information.
The weighted factors used to score proposals: capability, cost, delivery dates, technical approach, experience, financial stability.
A selection method used when only one supplier can meet the technical requirements, for example because of a patent.
A set price for a clearly defined scope. Cost risk is on the seller. Used when the scope is well defined.
The buyer pays the seller's actual costs plus a fee. Cost risk is on the buyer. Used when scope is uncertain or the work is high risk.
The buyer pays for time and materials used at agreed rates. A hybrid of fixed-price and cost-reimbursable. For smaller jobs or unclear scope.
A target cost is set, and savings or overruns are shared between buyer and seller.
Firm fixed price; fixed price incentive fee (bonus for targets); fixed price with economic price adjustment (adjusts for inflation on long contracts).
Cost plus fixed fee; cost plus incentive fee (fee tied to targets); cost plus award fee (fee decided by the buyer's judgment).
Negotiation first, then mediation, then arbitration. Litigation is the last option.
Mediation: a neutral third party helps the parties reach their own agreement. Arbitration: the third party makes a binding decision.
A structured review of the procurement process and contracts for completeness, accuracy and effectiveness.
Tolerance: acceptable variation for the requirement. Control limits: three standard deviations either side of the mean, the variation expected from the process.
Choosing part of a population for inspection, instead of inspecting every item.
The organization's basic principles for quality. It comes from the organization, not the project.
RFI: asks for information. RFQ: asks for prices of standard items. RFP: asks for a proposed solution.
Technical guidelines applied in design to optimize one aspect of the product: reliability, assembly, manufacturing, cost, service, usability, safety.
Checking that each seller's proposal is complete and responds in full to the bid documents, the statement of work and the selection criteria.
Deciding during planning how the product will be tested or inspected: alpha and beta tests, strength tests, field tests.
